newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA STALS TALKS ON "BIG BANG" FX LIFTING - PAPER.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA STALS TALKS ON "BIG BANG" FX LIFTING - PAPER.

text.p: South African Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals has spelled out the measures which would have to be in place for the country to contemplate a "big bang" lifting of exchange controls, the Business Day newspaper said on Wednesday.
Stals told the paper three conditions would have to be in place for him to consider recommending a one-off scrapping of exchange controls on residents -- the so-called "big bang" option.

Firstly, South Africa would need to have foreign credit lines of about 15 billion rand in place to finance the expected currency outflow. An International Monetary Fund credit of about $2 billion could form part of the facilities, although this would have to be linked to current account support.

Secondly, a package of broad economic measures -- "basically a restructuring programme" -- would have to be announced and implemented simultaneously. Stals said South Africa's macro-economic strategy had received IMF approval but the country might have to go further if it wanted to keep capital after lifting controls.

Thirdly, there had to be thorough consideration of the consequences of a one-off lifting of controls: "We have to be sure we can live with it. We cannot get cold feet if we see interest rates have to rise...I agree that things will be better in the long run if we do it, but we have to live that long."

If these key conditions were in place, the main question would be how long it would take before the country started experiencing net capital inflows. "I would be relatively optimistic that things could go well. But we would have to be well prepared," he said.
Stals said present policy was to build up reserves so that South Africa could take small steps to ease controls. "Our biggest problem is the fact that we do not have enough reserves," he said.
South Africa could speed up the process if it "steeled" itself for the consequences and was able to offer the right package of measures.
The country's meagre gold and foreign exchange reserves are expected to have been drained further in October, a casualty of the ailing rand.
Economists polled by Reuters forecast gross reserves would decline to 9.6 billion rand from 10 billion rand in September, equivalent to just under four weeks import cover.
October reserves will be released at 1600 GMT on Thursday.
